title: CBSE Class 10 English Language and Literature · Practice paper 3
subject: English Language and Literature
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper contains 24 questions. All questions are compulsory.

The question paper is divided into three sections:
Section A: Reading Skills (20 marks), questions 1 and 2
Section B: Grammar and Creative Writing Skills (20 marks), questions 3 to 14
Section C: Literature (40 marks), questions 15 to 24

The board paper has 11 questions. Here they are numbered so that each task can be answered and marked on its own: questions 3 to 12 are the grammar tasks of board question 3; question 13 is the letter (board question 4); question 14 is the analytical paragraph (board question 5); questions 15 and 16 are the extract-based questions (board questions 6 and 7); questions 17 to 20 are from First Flight (board question 8); questions 21 and 22 are from Footprints without Feet (board question 9); questions 23 and 24 are the long answer questions (board questions 10 and 11).
Answer the short answer questions (17 to 22) in about 40-50 words each, and the letter, the analytical paragraph and the long answer questions (23 and 24) in about 100-120 words each.

There are internal choices, marked OR, as in the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27: attempt any one of the two in question 13 (letter), question 14 (analytical paragraph), questions 15 and 16 (extract A or extract B: answer all the parts on the extract you choose) and questions 23 and 24 (long answers).

Where the board paper says 'attempt any ten of twelve' (grammar), 'any four of five' (First Flight) or 'any two of three' (Footprints without Feet), this paper gives the extra questions as OR choices for questions 8 and 11, question 20 and question 22.
Survey figures, names and places in the reading passages and the writing tasks are imaginary and created for practice.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

(1) Most of us remember the sinking feeling of a red mark on an answer sheet. From an early age, we learn to see a mistake as something to hide, a small stain on our record. Schools reward the right answer, parents celebrate full marks, and many students would rather leave a question blank than risk getting it wrong. But this fear of failure may be costing young people far more than a few marks.

(2) Think of how a baby learns to walk. She stands, wobbles and falls, again and again. No one calls her a failure; everyone understands that each fall teaches her a little more about balance. Somewhere between the playground and the examination hall, we forget this simple lesson. We begin to believe that clever people get things right the first time, and that a mistake proves we are not good enough.

(3) Studies of how people learn tell a different story. When students are asked to attempt a problem before they are taught how to solve it, they often struggle and make errors. Yet the same students frequently understand the topic more deeply later, because the struggle has prepared their minds to notice what matters. A mistake, looked at carefully, shows exactly where our understanding breaks down. It is less a verdict than a map.

(4) Of course, not every failure is useful. A mistake teaches us something only if we stop to ask why it happened. A student who glances at a wrong answer, sighs and turns the page has gained nothing. One who goes back, finds the faulty step and tries again has gained a great deal. The difference lies not in the mistake itself but in what we do with it.

(5) Many of the things we rely on every day came out of repeated failure. Engineers test materials until they find the point at which they break. Scientists run experiments that fail for years before one finally works. Even great writers fill wastepaper baskets with drafts before they produce a page they are proud of. In each case, failure is treated not as the end of the road but as useful information.

(6) Perhaps the most valuable thing we can teach young people, then, is not how to avoid mistakes but how to recover from them. That means praising effort and improvement, not only results; giving students the chance to correct their work; and admitting our own errors openly. A classroom where it is safe to be wrong is, in the end, a classroom where people learn to be right.

parts.q: (i) In paragraph 1, what does the detail that many students 'would rather leave a question blank than risk getting it wrong' suggest about them?
parts.model: It suggests that their fear of being wrong is so strong that they would rather not try at all.

points.t: Their fear of making a mistake is so strong that they avoid trying at all

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following with the correct option from the two given.
When the writer says that a mistake 'is less a verdict than a map' (paragraph 3), the writer means that a mistake ________.
(a) shows us where our understanding breaks down and so guides what we should learn next
(b) is a final judgement on how able a student really is
parts.model: (a) shows us where our understanding breaks down and so guides what we should learn next. [The paragraph says a mistake 'shows exactly where our understanding breaks down'; a map guides, while a verdict is a final judgement.]

points.t: Option (a)

parts.q:
(iii) Which of the following students uses a mistake in the way the writer recommends in paragraph 4?
A. Ravi tears up his test paper so that no one sees his low marks.
B. Neha copies the correct answer from a friend's notebook without reading it.
C. Arun reworks a wrong sum, finds the step where he went wrong and tries a similar sum.
D. Simran decides that she is simply not good at mathematics.
parts.model: C. Arun reworks a wrong sum, finds the step where he went wrong and tries a similar sum. [Paragraph 4: the student who 'goes back, finds the faulty step and tries again' gains a great deal.]

points.t: Option C

parts.q: (iv) Why does the writer describe how a baby learns to walk in paragraph 2?
parts.model: The example shows that falling, or making mistakes, is a natural and necessary part of learning: each fall teaches the baby a little more about balance, and no one calls her a failure. The writer uses it to contrast this with the way we later treat mistakes in school, as proof that we are not good enough.

points.t: Mistakes/falls are a natural part of learning: each fall teaches the baby something, and no one calls her a failure
Contrast with how we later see mistakes at school, as proof that we are not good enough

parts.q:
(v) State whether the following statement is True or False. (Paragraph 5)
The writer suggests that when an experiment fails, scientists should treat it as a sign to give up.
parts.model: False. [The writer says failure is treated 'not as the end of the road but as useful information'.]

points.t: False

parts.q:
(vi) Complete the analogy by selecting the correct option, (a) or (b).
a fall : a baby learning to walk :: ________ : an engineer testing a material
(a) the point at which the material breaks
(b) a material that never breaks
parts.model: (a) the point at which the material breaks. [A fall teaches the baby about balance; finding the breaking point teaches the engineer about the material. In both, the 'failure' gives useful information.]

points.t: Option (a)

parts.q:
(vii) Read the statements (i)-(v) and select the option that correctly classifies them as Facts (F) or Opinions (O).
(i) A baby who is learning to walk falls many times.
(ii) A classroom where it is safe to be wrong is a classroom where people learn to be right.
(iii) Engineers test materials until they find the point at which they break.
(iv) The most valuable thing we can teach young people is how to recover from mistakes.
(v) Some experiments fail for years before one finally works.
A. (i) F (ii) O (iii) F (iv) O (v) F
B. (i) F (ii) F (iii) O (iv) O (v) F
C. (i) O (ii) O (iii) F (iv) O (v) F
D. (i) F (ii) O (iii) F (iv) F (v) O
parts.model: A. (i) F (ii) O (iii) F (iv) O (v) F

points.t: Option A

parts.q: (viii) According to paragraph 6, what can adults do to help young people treat mistakes as useful? Mention any two ways.
parts.model: Adults can praise effort and improvement, not only results, and give students the chance to correct their work. They can also admit their own errors openly, so that the classroom becomes a place where it is safe to be wrong.

points.t: Any one way from paragraph 6: praise effort and improvement, not only results
A second way: give students the chance to correct their work / admit their own errors openly (a classroom where it is safe to be wrong)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

(1) In July 2026, Nandini Vidyalaya, a school of 800 students in Hirapur, began a 'Zero-Waste Lunch' drive. Students were asked to bring food in reusable boxes, carry steel bottles and avoid packaged snacks. To see whether the drive was working, the school's eco-club weighed the waste collected from all the classrooms after lunch.

(2) The table compares the waste collected on one school day in June, before the drive began, with the waste collected on one school day in October, three months later.
Type of wasteJune (kg)October (kg)
Plastic wrappers and packets124
Paper and tetra packs85
Leftover food106
Plastic bottles61
Total3616


(3) The biggest fall was in plastic. Members of the eco-club say that packets of chips and biscuits, once common in lunch boxes, are now rarely seen. Plastic bottles have almost disappeared because steel bottles can be refilled at the school's water coolers.

(4) Leftover food has proved harder to reduce. Teachers found that many students threw away food they did not like. The school now asks students to take home whatever they cannot finish, so that parents know what their children actually eat.

(5) The drive has also had an unexpected benefit. Classrooms are cleaner after lunch, and the cleaning staff spend less time sweeping. The eco-club now hopes to bring the total below 10 kg by March 2027 and to take the drive to the school canteen as well.

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence by selecting the correct option from those given in the bracket.
The word 'reusable' in paragraph 1 describes lunch boxes that ________. (can be used again and again / are thrown away after one use)
parts.model: can be used again and again

points.t: can be used again and again

parts.q: (ii) Why did the eco-club weigh the lunch-time waste? (Paragraph 1)
parts.model: To see whether the drive was working, that is, to find out whether the amount of waste had come down.

points.t: To check whether the drive was working / whether the waste had reduced

parts.q:
(iii) Select the option that is true for the assertion and reason given below.
Assertion: Paper and tetra packs showed the largest fall of all the types of waste.
Reason: The drive asked students to avoid packaged snacks.
A. Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation.
B. Both are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation.
C. The assertion is true, but the reason is false.
D. The assertion is false, but the reason is true.
parts.model: D. The assertion is false, but the reason is true. [Paper and tetra packs fell by only 3 kg (8 to 5), while plastic wrappers fell by 8 kg (12 to 4). The drive did ask students to avoid packaged snacks.]

points.t: Option D

parts.q:
(iv) Choose the correct option to complete the sentence.
All of the following are true according to the table EXCEPT ________.
A. Plastic wrappers and packets fell to one-third of the June figure.
B. In October, leftover food was the largest type of waste.
C. The total waste in October was less than half of the June total.
D. Paper and tetra packs fell by more than plastic bottles did.
parts.model: D. Paper and tetra packs fell by more than plastic bottles did. [Paper and tetra packs fell by 3 kg; plastic bottles fell by 5 kg. A is true: 4 is one-third of 12. B is true: 6 kg is the largest October figure. C is true: 16 is less than 18, half of 36.]

points.t: Option D

parts.q: (v) Compare the fall in plastic waste (wrappers and bottles together) with the fall in leftover food. What does this suggest? (Paragraphs 2-4)
parts.model: Plastic waste fell from 18 kg (12 + 6) to 5 kg (4 + 1), a fall of 13 kg, while leftover food fell only from 10 kg to 6 kg, a fall of 4 kg. This suggests that changing what students bring, such as packets and bottles, is easier than changing what they like to eat.

points.t: Correct comparison: plastic 18 kg to 5 kg (fall of 13 kg) against leftover food 10 kg to 6 kg (fall of 4 kg)
Inference: changing packaging/what students bring is easier than changing eating habits or tastes

parts.q:
(vi) Complete the sentence suitably. (Paragraph 3)
Plastic bottles have almost disappeared because ________.
parts.model: steel bottles can be refilled at the school's water coolers

points.t: steel bottles can be refilled at the school's water coolers

parts.q: (vii) Identify the phrase from paragraph 5 which shows that the drive brought a good result that no one had planned for.
parts.model: 'an unexpected benefit'

points.t: an unexpected benefit

parts.q: (viii) A parent finds that her son's lunch box often comes home half full. Based on paragraph 4, how does the school's new rule help her?
parts.model: Because the uneaten food now comes home, she can see what her son actually eats and what he leaves, so she can pack food he will eat and less is wasted.

points.t: She learns what her son actually eats/leaves, so she can pack food he will eat (less waste)

parts.q: (ix) Suggest one reason why 'Lighter Bins, Cleaner Classrooms' is a suitable title for the passage.
parts.model: It sums up the two results of the drive: the lunch-time waste fell from 36 kg to 16 kg, and the classrooms are cleaner after lunch.

points.t: Links the title to the content: waste fell (36 kg to 16 kg) and classrooms became cleaner

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the correct option to complete the line from a school announcement.
The new library block ________ by the Chief Guest next Monday.
questions.sol: The block does not perform the action, so the passive is needed, and 'next Monday' needs the future: 'will be inaugurated'. 'Was inaugurated' is past; 'has inaugurated' and 'is inaugurating' are active.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Report Rohan's statement by completing the sentence.
Rohan said to me, "I have lost my library card."
Rohan told me ________.
questions.model: Rohan told me that he had lost his library card.

points.t: that he had lost his library card

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank.
There isn't ________ sugar in the jar, so please buy some on your way home.
questions.sol: 'Sugar' is an uncountable noun, and in a negative sentence 'any' is used. 'Many', 'few' and 'a few' go with countable nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Identify the error in the given line from a lost-and-found notice and supply the correction.
The bunch of keys were found under a bench near the main gate.
Use the format: Error | Correction

points.t: Error: were; Correction: was (the subject is 'bunch', which is singular)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the correct option to complete the sentence from a sports report.
When he was only five, Arjun ________ swim across the pool without any help.
questions.sol: 'Could' expresses ability in the past ('when he was only five'). 'Can' is present; 'must' and 'should' express obligation and advice, not ability.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Report the tailor's question by completing the sentence.
The tailor asked Mr Rao, "When do you want the suit?"
The tailor asked Mr Rao ________.
questions.model: The tailor asked Mr Rao when he wanted the suit.

points.t: when he wanted the suit

or.text:
Report the doctor's question by completing the sentence.
The doctor asked Mr Iyer, "How long have you had this cough?"
The doctor asked Mr Iyer ________.
or.model: The doctor asked Mr Iyer how long he had had that cough.

points.t: how long he had had that cough (accept 'the cough')

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
The given sentence has an error. Select the option that correctly identifies the error and the correction.
My aunt has been living in Shimla since twelve years.
questions.sol: 'For' is used with a period of time (twelve years); 'since' is used with a point of time (since 2015).

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb given in the bracket.
While I ________ (walk) to school this morning, I saw a peacock on the wall.

points.t: was walking

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Fill in the blank by choosing the correct option from those given in the bracket.
________ student in the class received a certificate for taking part. (Every / All)

points.t: Every

or.text:
Fill in the blank by choosing the correct option from those given in the bracket.
________ of the two roads goes to the fort, so we will have to walk up the hill path. (Either / Neither)

points.t: Neither

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the option that correctly reports Neha's question.
Neha said to her mother, "Can I go to the fair with my friends?"
options: Neha asked her mother if she could go to the fair with her friends.
Neha asked her mother can she go to the fair with her friends.
Neha asked her mother that could she go to the fair with her friends.
Neha told her mother if she can go to the fair with her friends.
questions.sol: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', in statement order, and 'can' changes to 'could'. 'Told' does not introduce a question, and 'that' is not used before a reported question.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Attempt any one of the two, A or B.

A. You are Riya/Rohit Sen, 14 Lake Town, Kolkata. On 5 January 2027 you bought a study lamp from the online store of BrightHome Stores, Kolkata (Order No. BH2027/1145). It stopped working within a week. Write a letter in about 120 words to the Customer Care Manager, complaining about the defective lamp and requesting a replacement or a refund.
questions.model:
14 Lake Town
Kolkata
18 January 2027

The Customer Care Manager
BrightHome Stores
Kolkata

Subject: Complaint about a defective study lamp (Order No. BH2027/1145)

Sir/Madam

I am writing to complain about a study lamp that I bought from your online store on 5 January 2027.

The lamp was delivered on time, but it stopped working after only a week. The switch has become loose and the light flickers and then goes off. I have checked the plug and the socket, so the fault is in the lamp itself. As my board examinations are near, this has caused me great inconvenience.

The lamp carries a one-year warranty. I therefore request you to replace it at the earliest, or refund the amount of Rs 1,250. A copy of the bill is enclosed.

I hope for a prompt reply.

Yours faithfully
Riya Sen

points.t: Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, complimentary close and name, all in the correct places
Content: the complaint is stated with details (product, date of purchase, order number, the fault)
Content: the action wanted is stated clearly (replacement or refund, under warranty; bill enclosed)
Organisation: ideas in logical paragraphs (purpose, details of the problem, request, closing) joined with suitable linkers
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct and the tone is formal and polite

or.text: B. You are Ananya/Arnav Ghosh, 9 Civil Lines, Jaipur. Loudspeakers and DJ systems are often played till late at night during functions in your area, close to homes, schools and a hospital. Write a letter in about 120 words to the Editor of a local daily, drawing attention to the problem, its effects on residents and the steps that should be taken.
or.model:
9 Civil Lines
Jaipur
18 January 2027

The Editor
The Pink City Chronicle
Jaipur

Subject: Loud music late at night in residential areas

Sir/Madam

Through the columns of your newspaper, I wish to draw attention to the loud music played late at night in our residential areas.

During weddings and other functions, loudspeakers and DJ systems often play till well past midnight. The noise disturbs the sleep of children, who have to wake early for school, and of elderly and sick people. Patients in the nearby hospital suffer the most. Constant loud noise can also cause stress, headaches and even damage to hearing.

The authorities should strictly enforce the time limits on loudspeakers and fine those who break the rules. Residents, too, should celebrate considerately and keep the volume low.

I hope this letter will lead to prompt action.

Yours faithfully
Ananya Ghosh

points.t: Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, complimentary close and name, all in the correct places
Content: the problem is described (loud music late at night near homes, schools and a hospital)
Content: its effects (sleep, students, the elderly and patients, health) and at least two steps to be taken (enforce time limits, fines, considerate celebration)
Organisation: ideas in logical paragraphs (purpose, problem and effects, suggestions, closing) joined with suitable linkers
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct and the tone is formal

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Attempt any one of the two, A or B.

A. The table shows how the Class 10 students of Green Park School spent their pocket money in 2023 and in 2026. Write an analytical paragraph in about 120 words analysing the changes.
Item20232026
Snacks and fast food35%25%
Mobile recharges and apps15%28%
Stationery and books20%22%
Savings20%15%
Gifts and others10%10%
questions.model: The table shows how Class 10 students of Green Park School spent their pocket money in 2023 and in 2026. In 2023, snacks and fast food took the largest share, at 35%, but by 2026 this had fallen to 25%. The most striking change is the rise in spending on mobile recharges and apps, which nearly doubled, from 15% to 28%, making it the largest item in 2026. In contrast, savings fell from 20% to 15%. Spending on stationery and books rose slightly, from 20% to 22%, while gifts and other items stayed steady at 10%. Overall, the data shows a clear shift from food towards digital spending, and the fall in savings is a cause for concern.

points.t: Content: the key changes are reported with correct figures (e.g. snacks 35% to 25%, mobile and apps 15% to 28%, savings 20% to 15%)
Content: an overall trend or conclusion is drawn (e.g. a shift from food to digital spending; falling savings), not just a list of figures
Organisation: an introductory sentence and a concluding statement; no title
Organisation: points in a logical order, linked with words of comparison (in contrast, while, overall)
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

or.text:
B. Your school is discussing whether printed textbooks should be replaced with tablets. Study the notes below and write an analytical paragraph in about 120 words, evaluating whether this is a good idea.
Advantages: lighter school bags; videos and animations explain difficult topics; books can be updated quickly; saves paper
Disadvantages: tablets are costly; not all families have internet; strain on the eyes; distraction by games; a broken or uncharged tablet stops learning
or.model: Some schools are considering replacing printed textbooks with tablets, and the idea has both strengths and weaknesses. On the one hand, a single tablet can hold all the books, so school bags become lighter. Tablets can also show videos and animations that make difficult topics easier to understand, and digital books can be updated quickly. Moreover, saving paper helps the environment. On the other hand, tablets are costly, and not every family can afford one or pay for an internet connection. Long hours of screen use can strain the eyes, and students may be distracted by games. Besides, a broken or uncharged tablet can stop learning altogether. On balance, tablets can support printed books, but they should not replace them completely until these problems are solved.

points.t: Content: the advantages are analysed using the notes (lighter bags, videos, quick updates, saving paper)
Content: the disadvantages are analysed (cost, internet, eye strain, distraction, breakdown) and a reasoned judgement is given
Organisation: an introductory sentence and a concluding statement; no title
Organisation: points in a logical order, linked with words such as on the one hand, moreover, on the other hand, on balance
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the given extracts A and B and answer ANY ONE of the two. Answer all the parts on the extract you choose: the main parts are on extract A, and their OR parts are on extract B.

A.
Sitting down, she looked to see who had spoken. It was an elderly man who had honestly been concerned for her, but she was annoyed by his attention.
"There's nobody here who's a child," she said haughtily. "I've paid my thirty paise like everyone else."
The conductor chimed in. "Oh, sir, but this is a very grown-up madam. Do you think a mere girl could pay her own fare and travel to the city all alone?"
Valli shot an angry glance at the conductor and said, "I am not a madam. Please remember that. And you've not yet given me my ticket."
"I'll remember," the conductor said, mimicking her tone. Everyone laughed, and gradually Valli too joined in the laughter.
(Madam Rides the Bus, Vallikkannan)

OR

B.
So the world is afflicted with death and decay, therefore the wise do not grieve, knowing the terms of the world.
"Not from weeping nor from grieving will anyone obtain peace of mind; on the contrary, his pain will be the greater and his body will suffer. He will make himself sick and pale, yet the dead are not saved by his lamentation. He who seeks peace should draw out the arrow of lamentation, and complaint, and grief."
(The Sermon at Benares)

parts.q:
(i) [Extract A] Complete the sentence suitably.
Valli is annoyed by the elderly man's concern because ________.
parts.model: she does not want to be treated as a child; she has paid her own fare like everyone else and sees herself as a grown-up

points.t: she does not want to be treated as a child / she has paid her fare like everyone else and sees herself as grown-up

or.q:
(i) [Extract B] Complete the sentence suitably.
According to the Buddha, the wise do not grieve because ________.
or.model: they know the terms of the world: the world is afflicted with death and decay, and all who are born must die

points.t: they know the terms of the world / that death and decay come to all

parts.q:
(ii) [Extract A] Choose the correct option.
The conductor's words, 'this is a very grown-up madam', are spoken ________.
A. angrily, to scold Valli for being rude
B. in a teasing, light-hearted way
C. respectfully, because he thinks Valli is an important lady
D. sadly, because he pities Valli
parts.model: B. in a teasing, light-hearted way [The conductor is 'a jolly sort, fond of joking'; the passengers laugh with him.]

points.t: Option B

or.q:
(ii) [Extract B] Choose the correct option.
The Buddha speaks of 'the arrow of lamentation' because grief ________.
A. helps a person to aim at a higher goal
B. is like a wound that keeps hurting until it is drawn out
C. can be used to protect the dead
D. passes quickly, like an arrow in flight
or.model: B. is like a wound that keeps hurting until it is drawn out [He says that he who seeks peace should draw out the arrow; only then does one become composed.]

points.t: Option B

parts.q:
(iii) [Extract A] Fill in the blank with the correct option from the bracket.
The word 'haughtily' shows that Valli spoke ________. (proudly / politely)
parts.model: proudly

points.t: proudly

or.q:
(iii) [Extract B] Fill in the blank with the correct option from the bracket.
'Afflicted with death and decay' means that the world is ________ by death and decay. (troubled / untouched)

points.t: troubled

parts.q: (iv) [Extract A] What does Valli's joining in the laughter at the end of the extract tell us about her?
parts.model: Valli is proud and touchy about being treated as a child, and at first she is angry with the conductor. But her anger does not last: she can laugh at herself and share the joke. This shows that she has a sense of humour and is beginning to relax and enjoy her first bus ride.

points.t: Though proud and touchy about being called a child, her anger is short-lived
She has a sense of humour / can laugh at herself; she relaxes and begins to enjoy the ride

or.q: (iv) [Extract B] Why, according to the Buddha, does weeping help neither the mourner nor the dead? Answer with reference to the extract.
or.model: Weeping brings the mourner no peace of mind: his pain becomes greater, his body suffers and he makes himself sick and pale. Nor does it help the dead, who are not saved by his lamentation. So one who seeks peace should draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint and grief.

points.t: For the mourner: no peace of mind; his pain is greater, his body suffers, he grows sick and pale
For the dead: they are not saved by lamentation, so grief is of no use (draw out the arrow of grief)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the given extracts A and B and answer ANY ONE of the two. Answer all the parts on the extract you choose: the main parts are on extract A, and their OR parts are on extract B.

A.
If strolling forth, a beast you view,
Whose hide with spots is peppered,
As soon as he has lept on you,
You'll know it is the Leopard.
'Twill do no good to roar with pain,
He'll only lep and lep again.
(How to Tell Wild Animals, Carolyn Wells)

OR

B.
I thought I told you to clean your shoes,
Amanda!
(I am an orphan, roaming the street.
I pattern soft dust with my hushed, bare feet.
The silence is golden, the freedom is sweet.)
(Amanda!, Robin Klein)

parts.q:
(i) [Extract A] Complete the sentence suitably.
According to the poet, you will know that the beast is a leopard ________.
parts.model: only when it has leapt on you

points.t: only when/as soon as it has leapt on you

or.q:
(i) [Extract B] Complete the sentence suitably.
The line 'I thought I told you to clean your shoes' shows that the speaker is ________.
or.model: irritated that her instructions have not been obeyed (she keeps nagging Amanda)

points.t: irritated / annoyed that her instructions are not obeyed; nagging

parts.q:
(ii) [Extract A] Choose the correct option.
The lines ''Twill do no good to roar with pain, / He'll only lep and lep again' suggest that once the leopard attacks, ________.
A. the victim can frighten it away by shouting
B. crying out will not save the victim; it will only attack again
C. the leopard will feel sorry for the victim
D. the leopard will run back into the jungle
parts.model: B. crying out will not save the victim; it will only attack again

points.t: Option B

or.q:
(ii) [Extract B] Choose the correct option.
The word 'hushed' in 'my hushed, bare feet' suggests that Amanda's footsteps are ________.
A. loud and heavy
B. quick and nervous
C. soft and quiet
D. slow and painful
or.model: C. soft and quiet [Hushed means silent or quiet; it fits 'The silence is golden'.]

points.t: Option C

parts.q:
(iii) [Extract A] Fill in the blank with the correct option from the bracket.
In 'Whose hide with spots is peppered', the word 'peppered' means ________. (thickly dotted / badly torn)
parts.model: thickly dotted

points.t: thickly dotted

or.q:
(iii) [Extract B] Fill in the blank with ONE suitable word.
In 'The silence is golden', Amanda shows that she treasures the ________ of being left alone.

points.t: peace / quiet / calm

parts.q: (iv) [Extract A] Why is the poet's way of identifying the leopard absurd, and how does this create humour?
parts.model: The poet says you will know the beast is a leopard only after it has leapt on you, when the knowledge is of no use, so the advice is absurd. The humour comes from this mock-serious advice and from the playful language, such as a hide 'peppered' with spots and the leopard that will 'lep and lep again'.

points.t: Absurd: you identify the leopard only when it attacks you, when the knowledge is useless
Humour from mock-serious advice and playful language ('peppered', 'lep and lep again')

or.q: (iv) [Extract B] How does the poet use the two voices in the extract to show the gap between the speaker and Amanda?
or.model: The first voice is the adult's: a reminder ending in an exclamation, 'Amanda!', which shows constant nagging. Amanda's voice is in brackets: she does not answer aloud but escapes into a dream of being a free orphan. The contrast shows that she is not listening and that she longs for freedom from control.

points.t: The adult's voice: reminders and exclamations show constant nagging/control
Amanda's voice in brackets: unspoken daydream of freedom; she is not listening, and wants to escape control

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Mandela says that the air show at his inauguration was 'not only a display of pinpoint precision and military force'. What else did the air show and the generals' salute show, and why did the salute mean so much to him? (Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom)
questions.model: The jets, helicopters and troop carriers roaring in perfect formation showed the military's loyalty to democracy, to a new government that had been freely and fairly elected. The highest generals of the defence force and police saluted Mandela and pledged their loyalty. He knew that not so many years before they would have arrested him, not saluted him: South Africa had truly changed.

points.t: Content: the air show showed the military's loyalty to democracy / to a freely and fairly elected government
Content: the generals saluted him and pledged loyalty, though a few years before they would have arrested him: a sign of how the country had changed

questions.subject: English
questions.text: After his first flight, the young seagull came down to join his family on the sea. What happened when he landed, and how did his family greet him? (His First Flight)
questions.model: His family had landed on the green sea ahead of him and were calling to him. When he dropped his legs to stand on it, they sank in. He screamed with fright and tried to rise, but he was tired and weak with hunger. Then his belly touched the sea and he floated. His family screamed around him, praising him and offering him scraps of dog-fish.

points.t: Content: his legs sank into the 'green sea'; he screamed with fright, could not rise (tired, weak with hunger), then floated
Content: his family screamed around him, praising him and offering him scraps of dog-fish

questions.subject: English
questions.text: 'For Anne Gregory' is a conversation in three stanzas. Who speaks in each stanza, and how does each stanza answer the one before it? (For Anne Gregory, W. B. Yeats)
questions.model: In the first stanza the young man tells Anne that young men will love her only for her yellow hair, never for herself alone. In the second, Anne answers that she can dye her hair brown, black or carrot so that she is loved for herself. In the third, he replies that an old religious man had found a text to prove that only God could love her so.

points.t: Content: stanza 1, the young man: young men will love her yellow hair, not her; stanza 2, Anne: she can dye it brown, black or carrot to be loved for herself
Content: stanza 3, the young man again: an old religious man's text proves that only God can love her for herself alone (each stanza answers the last)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: How did the narrator of 'The Black Aeroplane' feel inside the storm, and why did he follow the strange aeroplane 'like an obedient child'? (Two Stories about Flying)
questions.model: Inside the storm everything was suddenly black; the old Dakota jumped and twisted, and the compass, the other instruments and the radio were all dead. He was lost and frightened. When the strange aeroplane appeared and its pilot waved, 'Follow me', he was very happy to follow, because he had no radio, no compass and no other way to find his way, and he was on his last fuel tank.

points.t: Content: in the storm: everything black, the plane jumped and twisted, compass, instruments and radio dead; he was lost and afraid
Content: he followed because he had no other help or way to navigate (on his last fuel tank); the pilot waved 'Follow me'

or.text: In her diary entry of 20 June 1942, Anne writes that her whole class is 'quaking in its boots'. What were her classmates doing, and what does her account of them show about Anne? (From the Diary of Anne Frank)
or.model: The teachers were about to decide who would move up to the next form. Half the class was making bets, and two boys had staked their entire holiday savings. Anne and G.N. laughed themselves silly at them. Anne frankly says that a quarter of the class should be kept back, but she is sure that she and her friends will make it. This shows her humour and confidence.

points.t: Content: classmates: making bets on who would be kept back; two boys staked their holiday savings; Anne and G.N. laughed at them
Content: Anne: humorous, frank (about a quarter of the class should be kept back) and confident ('We'll make it')

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Being invisible did not make life easy for Griffin in a London winter. What happened when he spent a night in a big London store? (Footprints without Feet)
questions.model: It was mid-winter and bitterly cold, so Griffin slipped into a big store for warmth. After closing time he fitted himself out with warm clothes, ate cold meat, coffee and sweets, and slept on a pile of quilts. But he did not wake up until the assistants arrived. He panicked and ran, and escaped only by taking off his new clothes, naked again in the chill January air.

questions.subject: English
questions.text: What do Think-Tank's talk with his mirror and his demand to hear his full salutation show about him? How does this side of him help to save the Earth? (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.model: Think-Tank is vain and conceited. He makes Noodle repeat his whole salutation, asks his mirror who is the most 'intellectually gifted being in the land', scolds it for answering slowly and boasts of his 'balloon brain'. Sure of his own wisdom, he never doubts his reading of the nursery rhymes, so when Humpty Dumpty seems to look like him, he panics and orders Mars to be evacuated.

points.t: Content: vain and conceited: the full salutation, the mirror ('I hate a slow mirror'), his 'balloon brain'

or.text: Hari Singh says that Anil was 'the most trusting person' he had ever met, 'And that is why it was so difficult to rob him.' Explain what he means. (The Thief's Story)
or.model: Anil had given Hari a key to the door, and he could come and go as he pleased. Hari felt that it is easy to rob a greedy man, because he can afford to be robbed, but difficult to rob a careless man, who sometimes does not even notice the theft. That, he says, takes all the pleasure out of the work.

points.t: Content: Anil trusted him completely: he gave Hari a key and let him come and go as he pleased
Content: a greedy man can afford to be robbed; a careless, trusting man may not even notice, which takes all the pleasure out of the work

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Attempt any one of the two, A or B, in about 100-120 words.

A. Custard the dragon and the young seagull are both looked down on as cowards. Compare how each is treated by those around him, what finally makes each of them act, and what the two texts suggest about courage. (The Tale of Custard the Dragon; His First Flight)
questions.model:
Custard and the young seagull are both seen as cowards. Belinda tickles Custard unmercifully, and Ink, Blink and Mustard rudely call him Percival while he cries for a nice safe cage. The seagull is left alone on his ledge; his family scold him, threaten to let him starve and taunt him with his cowardice.
Each acts only when need forces him. When a pirate climbs in at the window and the pets flee, Custard jumps up snorting like an engine and gobbles the pirate. The seagull, maddened by hunger, dives at the fish his mother holds out and finds that he can fly.
Both texts suggest that courage is often hidden until a real test comes. Custard stays modest, agreeing that everybody is braver than him, while the seagull is welcomed by his family.

points.t: Content: how each is treated: Custard tickled and called Percival, cries for a safe cage; the seagull scolded, threatened with starvation, taunted
Content: what makes each act: the pirate (the pets flee, Custard attacks and gobbles him); hunger and the fish (he dives and flies)
Content: what the texts suggest: courage is hidden until tested; Custard stays modest, the seagull is praised
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
Expression: the answer is fluent, relevant and in about 100-120 words
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

or.text: B. Both the tiger in 'A Tiger in the Zoo' and Amanda long for a freedom they do not have. Compare what holds each of them back, how each of them responds, and what the two poems suggest about freedom. (A Tiger in the Zoo; Amanda!)
or.model:
The tiger is held back by bars: locked in a concrete cell, he stalks the few steps of his cage in quiet rage when he should be lurking in shadow near the water hole. Amanda is held back by constant instructions and nagging about her nails, her homework, her shoes and her chocolate.
The tiger ignores the visitors and at night stares at the brilliant stars. Amanda escapes into daydreams: she imagines herself a mermaid drifting on a languid, emerald sea, an orphan roaming the street and Rapunzel in a tower. Her only open protest is sulking, which is called moodiness.
Both poems suggest that freedom is natural to every living being, and that a life of control, whether by bars or by endless orders, leads to silent anger and withdrawal.

points.t: Content: what holds each back: the tiger's concrete cell and bars; Amanda's constant instructions and nagging
Content: responses: the tiger's quiet rage, ignoring visitors, staring at the stars; Amanda's daydreams (mermaid, orphan, Rapunzel) and sulking
Content: what the poems suggest: freedom is natural; control or confinement leads to silent anger and withdrawal

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Attempt any one of the two, A or B, in about 100-120 words.

A. Griffin went to Iping to be left alone, but his stay at the village inn ended in uproar. Trace the events at the inn, from his arrival to his escape. (Footprints without Feet)
questions.model:
Griffin took a train to Iping and booked two rooms at the inn. He told Mrs Hall that he wanted solitude and that an accident had affected his face. As he had paid in advance, she excused his strange habits and irritable temper as those of an eccentric scientist.
When his stolen money ran out, he pretended to be expecting a cheque. Then the housekeeping money vanished from a clergyman's study that seemed empty. Next morning the Halls found his room empty; his hat and a chair attacked them and pushed them out. When he suddenly produced cash, he was suspected of the burglary.
Confronted by Mrs Hall, he threw off his bandages, whiskers, spectacles and nose, and stood headless. The constable, Jaffers, tried to arrest him, but Griffin threw off his clothes, knocked Jaffers unconscious and escaped.

points.t: Content: arrival: two rooms; wants solitude, says an accident has affected his face; Mrs Hall excuses him (paid in advance, an eccentric scientist)
Content: money runs out (a cheque expected); the clergyman's burglary; the hat and chair attack the Halls; suspicion when he produces cash
Content: Mrs Hall confronts him; he throws off his disguise (a headless man); Jaffers knocked unconscious; Griffin escapes
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
Expression: the answer is fluent, relevant and in about 100-120 words
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

or.text: B. Bholi's parents saw her as a burden. Discuss how they treated her and planned her future, and how Bholi showed at the end that they had misjudged her. (Bholi)
or.model:
After a fall from her cot and an attack of small-pox, Bholi was a pock-marked girl who stammered, and everyone called her a simpleton. New clothes were never made for her, and no one cared to mend or wash her old ones.
She was sent to school only because the Tehsildar told Ramlal to set an example; her mother said there was little chance of her getting married, so the teachers could worry about her. Later her parents accepted Bishamber, a lame man nearly Ramlal's age, glad that he did not know about her pock-marks. Her mother called her a dumb cow.
At the wedding Bishamber demanded five thousand rupees. Bholi refused to marry such a mean, greedy and contemptible coward, and calmly said she would serve her parents and teach in her school. They had misjudged her.

points.t: Content: how she was treated: a pock-marked, stammering 'simpleton'; no new clothes, no care
Content: their plans: school only because of the Tehsildar ('Let the teachers at school worry about her'); the match with the lame, older Bishamber; 'a dumb cow'
Content: the end: she rejects the greedy Bishamber (five thousand rupees) and will serve her parents and teach: they had misjudged her
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
